name: Raghav
definition: Raghav is a composite portrait of a skilled industrial worker navigating the coastal economy where processing exports and service-sector growth shape household opportunity. He embodies the pressures facing households dependent on seasonal factory wages in a district known for high literacy yet where migration, private-school competition and economic volatility alter what families can afford to plan for their children.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Raghav supervises the second shift—afternoon through late evening—at a medium-sized cashew-processing unit on the edge of Udupi town, one of a cluster that feeds the Mangaluru export hub. His day begins around noon: checking the roasting drums, ensuring the women on the peeling line meet tonnage targets, troubleshooting machinery breakdowns that can idle fifty workers at once. The unit processes raw cashew from Kerala and local estates; peak season runs October through March, then work thins for four months. He earns about eighteen thousand rupees a month during the season, dropping to twelve when orders slow, plus a modest Diwali bonus if the export price holds. His employer is better than most—wages arrive on time, the factory has fire exits—but dust and heat are constants, and the peeling women, many migrants from north Karnataka, work for daily rates he knows are low. Raghav walks or rides a scooter the three kilometres from home; fuel and vehicle repair are monthly headaches. The job is stable by Udupi's processing-sector standards, but cashew prices swing with global demand and currency rates, so layoffs and short-time are always possible. He worries the younger generation sees only IT jobs in Manipal or Bengaluru and scorns shop-floor work.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Raghav lives with his wife Jyothi, their two children—a daughter in Class 9 and a son in Class 6—and his widowed mother in a small rented house in one of the older residential lanes near the Udupi market. Jyothi worked in a garment unit years ago but left after their son was born; she now stitches blouses at home for a neighbourhood boutique, earning three to four thousand rupees a month. His mother, in her late sixties, manages the cooking and watches the children after school, a presence Raghav depends on entirely because his shift ends at ten-thirty at night. His elder brother migrated to Mumbai two decades ago and works in a hotel; remittances have dwindled as his brother's own children's expenses climbed, so Raghav shoulders most of the household budget. Decisions about schooling, especially whether their daughter will continue to PU college and beyond, are made jointly by Raghav and Jyothi, though his mother's voice—rooted in older expectations about marriage timing—carries weight. Gender roles are traditional: Jyothi manages money, food and the children's homework; Raghav handles rent, school fees and any encounter with government offices. The house has two rooms, a narrow kitchen and an attached toilet; privacy is scarce and tensions over study space and screen time common.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Raghav completed his SSLC at a Kannada-medium government high school in a taluk town and tried first-year PU but dropped out when his father fell ill and income was needed; he has always regretted not finishing. His daughter attends a private English-medium school near the town centre—fees are about twenty-five thousand a year with books and uniform, a quarter of his annual earnings—while his son is in a less expensive Kannada-medium aided school, a compromise driven by cost. The daughter is a steady student; Raghav and Jyothi hope she will reach degree level and perhaps teacher training, though anxiety about PU college fees and hostel costs if she must study away looms large. Udupi town has many private schools, some backed by trusts with reputations stretching back generations; the government school nearby is poorly enrolled, its playground shared with a bus stand. Tuition is assumed necessary from Class 8 onward—another three thousand rupees a month the household can barely meet. His daughter has asked to study science in PU, which would require coaching Raghav knows he cannot afford without borrowing.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Health access in Udupi town is good on paper—a government taluk hospital, numerous private clinics and Manipal's big hospitals twenty minutes away by bus—but cost is the barrier. Raghav's mother has diabetes and high blood pressure; her monthly medication, even from a government hospital's pharmacy, costs about eight hundred rupees, and when supplies run out they buy from private chemists at double. A serious illness means referral to Manipal or Mangaluru, and while the household holds an Ayushman Bharat card, navigating the cashless system and securing a bed in empanelled hospitals has proven confusing and sometimes requires out-of-pocket deposits anyway. Jyothi suffered a complicated delivery with their son and needed a Caesarean at a private maternity home; they are still paying off that loan in small instalments to a relative. Raghav's work environment—heat, dust, noise—leaves him with a persistent cough he has never had properly investigated; factory health checks are cursory. The children are generally healthy, vaccinated through government drives at school, though dental care is unaffordable unless pain becomes unbearable. Household water comes from a municipal tap, safe enough, though summer shortages mean buying tanker water some years. Mental-health vocabulary is absent; stress and exhaustion are borne silently. The cashew factory has no health insurance scheme for supervisors, and accident or injury would devastate the family budget immediately.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Raghav's family is Hindu, loosely tied to a neighbourhood temple dedicated to a local deity where his mother goes for monthly pujas; there is no strong caste-organisation membership or ritual leadership role. Udupi town's public culture is visibly diverse—Jain basadis, the Krishna Matha complex, churches, mosques—but daily socialising remains within broad religious lines. Raghav has Muslim and Christian co-workers at the factory; relations are cordial, professional, with no memory of personal friction, though he is aware that communal rhetoric surfaces around elections and sometimes at college campuses. He does not participate in any Bhuta Kola or Yakshagana events personally, though he respects them as important local tradition and took his children once to a Yakshagana performance at Kateel. Social ties are anchored in the neighbourhood lane—borrowing, shared wedding invitations, children's friendships—and in the loose network of factory colleagues. His mother's generation speaks of communal harmony as Udupi's strength, yet Raghav has heard grumbles among co-workers after moral-policing incidents reported in Udayavani about couples harassed near the beach or college students targeted, discomfort that it tarnishes the town's image. The family has no land, no CAMPCO membership, no Gulf relatives—so the kinship safety nets that cushion other Udupi households are missing. Community is functional, not deep; support is neighbour-to-neighbour, case-by-case.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Raghav's encounters with government are mostly bureaucratic frustrations. Obtaining his mother's diabetes medication requires monthly queues at the taluk hospital pharmacy, where stock-outs are common and counters open late. The family's ration card is functional—they draw subsidised rice and kerosene—but Aadhaar-linking glitches have caused payment delays twice, requiring hours at the taluk office to resolve. His children's school certificates and his own SSLC documents needed for a bank-loan application took weeks and small bribes to extract from the education-department record room. He has never attended a gram sabha or municipal ward meeting; politics feels distant, something decided by larger players. The Shakti free-bus scheme has been a real gain for Jyothi and his daughter, cutting travel cost for tuition and hospital visits. He has heard of Ayushman Bharat but finds the enrollment process and hospital empanelment opaque. No one in the household receives a pension or MGNREGA wages; the labour-department helpline for factory-worker grievances exists in theory but he would never risk his supervisor post by filing a complaint. Local municipal services—garbage collection, street lights—are acceptable in his lane, worse in the poorer migrant-labour colonies near the factory.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Raghav is proud that his children are studying in better schools than he did, and proud of Udupi's reputation—temples, Manipal's colleges, the cleanliness compared to other towns he has visited. But pride is shot through with anxiety: will his daughter's education lead to a job, or only to marriage and a demand for dowry he cannot meet? He worries about his own job security as younger men are willing to work for less, and worries that mechanisation or a bad export season could make him redundant. He blames no one villain but feels the system is rigged for those who already have—land, Gulf money, connections to get a government job. He respects education but resents its price, and resents that private schools treat parents like customers while government schools are seen as dumping grounds. He is angered by news of corruption and by the sight of political leaders' convoys while his lane's drainage remains broken, yet he does not believe any party will truly change things for a family like his. What he wants is stability—his job to continue, his daughter to finish PU without the family taking ruinous loans, his son to find some decent work, his mother's health to hold. He does not expect government help beyond ration and bus fare, but demands it function without humiliation: medicines in stock, certificates issued on time, school teachers who teach. He fears climate-linked disruption—floods have worsened in recent years, and one season the factory was waterlogged for a week—and fears the gap between his household and the Manipal-Mangaluru prosperity he sees around him will only widen.
